headline: Cannabis medicine calms agitation in dementia patients

sources.title: Combination of THC and CBD significantly reduced agitation in people with late-stage dementia
Clinical Trial: THC-CBD Formulation Reduces Agitation in Dementia Patients, With Nearly 90% Showing Improvement
Agitation improves in Alzheimer's disease with combined CBD, THC treatment
Study suggests cannabis compounds may help some dementia patients (video, CBS19)

chunks.text: Scientists have {{come up with}} a new medicine that may bring [[relief]] to people with [[late-stage]] dementia. The medicine [[carefully]] mixes two [[compounds]] from the cannabis plant, known as THC and CBD. Doctors tested it on patients who often [[deal with]] [[agitation]], a state of restlessness and [[distress]]. In early results that just {{came out}}, the treatment {{calmed down}} many patients.

verbs.correct: To invent or create something new
verbs.why: Engineers come up with a fix for a broken part, and a chef can come up with a new recipe overnight. Scientists have come up with a new medicine that mixes THC and CBD for people with late-stage dementia.

verbs.correct: To become known or be made public
verbs.why: Test scores come out a few weeks after an exam, and election results come out late at night. Early results from this dementia trial just came out, and they surprised many researchers.

verbs.correct: To make someone become less upset or less restless
verbs.wrong: To completely cure a person's long-term illness
verbs.why: A soft voice can calm down a scared child, and quiet music calms down a nervous dog before a storm. In the trial, the new medicine calmed down many patients who had been restless for months.

chunks.text: The researchers {{went about}} the LiBBY [[trial]] [[with great care]], testing about 120 people whose dementia was very [[advanced]]. Their [[average]] age was 80, and most were [[eligible]] for [[hospice]] care. Nurses {{handed out}} the medicine as a [[fast-acting]] oil that patients could swallow. For 12 weeks, the team {{kept track of}} how each person's behavior and mood changed.

verbs.correct: To begin or handle a task in a particular way
verbs.wrong: To travel or move around from place to place
verbs.why: A careful cook goes about a recipe step by step, and a good manager goes about a project with a clear plan. The research team went about the dementia trial with great care, testing about 120 patients.

verbs.correct: To give something to each person in a group
verbs.wrong: To give people advice or instructions
verbs.why: Teachers hand out papers at the start of class, and volunteers hand out water at a race. Nurses handed out the new medicine as a fast-acting oil for patients to swallow.

verbs.correct: To watch or follow something carefully over time
verbs.wrong: To move at the same speed as everyone else
verbs.why: A coach keeps track of every player's minutes, and a nurse keeps track of a patient's blood pressure. For 12 weeks, the research team kept track of how each patient's mood and behavior changed.

chunks.text: The results {{turned out}} to be very strong. Close to 90 percent of the patients on the medicine got better, while [[far fewer]] improved on a [[placebo]]. That large [[gap]] made the study {{jump out}} at other researchers. One lead doctor said it is [[rare]] to see so many patients respond so well to a new drug.

verbs.correct: To happen or end in a particular way
verbs.wrong: To produce or make something in large amounts
verbs.why: A rainy forecast can turn out sunny, and a nervous first date can turn out wonderfully. The results of this dementia trial turned out far stronger than most researchers expected.

verbs.correct: To be immediately noticeable or obvious
verbs.wrong: To physically leap through the air fast
verbs.why: A bright red coat can jump out in a gray crowd, and a bold headline jumps out on a page. The huge gap between the two groups made this study jump out at researchers everywhere.

chunks.text: Still, the researchers {{spell out}} that this is a controlled medical treatment, not the same as recreational cannabis products sold in stores. The medicine was made in a lab and given under close [[supervision]]. [[Side effects]] were [[mild]], and doctors could not {{rule out}} that some were caused by the illness itself. As they {{look ahead}}, the team hopes larger trials will [[confirm]] these [[hopeful]] results.

verbs.correct: To explain something clearly and in detail
verbs.wrong: To sum up a result in a few words
verbs.why: A good manual spells out each step, and a doctor spells out exactly how to take a new medicine. The researchers spell out that this treatment is a lab-made drug, not the cannabis sold in stores.

verbs.correct: To decide that something is not possible
verbs.wrong: To fully explain the reason for something
verbs.why: A mechanic rules out engine trouble before checking the tires, and a doctor rules out one illness before testing for another. Doctors in this trial could not rule out that some side effects came from the dementia itself.

verbs.correct: To think about or plan for the future
verbs.wrong: To feel excited and happy about a future event
verbs.why: A young couple looks ahead to buying a first home, and a coach looks ahead to next season's schedule. As they look ahead, the research team hopes larger trials will confirm these early results.

mainIdea.s: Scientists made a new medicine from two cannabis compounds for people with late-stage dementia and agitation. Close to 90 percent of those who took it improved, far more than those on a placebo.
mainIdea.why: The story says close to 90 percent of patients on the medicine improved, while far fewer improved on a placebo.

mainIdea.s: Scientists tested a new cannabis based medicine on people with early memory loss who still live alone at home. Close to 90 percent of them said they felt much calmer within the very first week.
mainIdea.why: The trial gave the medicine to late-stage dementia patients mostly in hospice care, not people with early memory loss living alone. Results came after 12 weeks, not the first week.

mainIdea.s: A separate research team in Canada is now testing a common blood pressure drug that may slow early signs of memory loss. The study does not involve cannabis or any patients in hospice care.
mainIdea.why: This is about a blood pressure drug study in Canada. The article is about a cannabis based medicine for agitation in late-stage dementia.
